text: the world.12 A report from the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa highlighted the risk for rapid death in HIV- infected persons with extensively-drug resistant tuberculo- sis.13 In this local case series, all but one of 53 patients died, and where the date of death could be confirmed the median survival was 16 days from the time of diagnosis. • Children and infants can be treated with regimens sim- ilar to adults but with appropriate dose adjustments for age or body-weight.4-7 While ethambutol is not usually given to young children because of the perceived difficulty in de- tecting ocular toxicity (see p.274), a literature review14 on its use in children found almost no ocular toxicity at daily doses of 15 to 30 mg/kg and it was considered safe in chil- dren of all ages. • Pregnancy, breast feeding, and the neonate. Tubercu- losis, and especially drug-resistant tuberculosis, during pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother, fetus, and ne- onate if not detected early and treated properly.15 The WHO recommends that pregnant women with tuberculo- sis are treated similarly to non-pregnant patients (RHZE2/RH4 or RHZ2/RH4). Fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, ethionamide, and protionamide are best avoided. Liver enzymes and symptoms of drug-induced hepatitis should be monitored.4,5,15 Most antituberculous drugs may be used during breast feeding. Drug concentra- tions in the breast milk are too low to prevent or treat tu- berculosis in infants. In the UK it is recommended that ne- onates of mothers with tuberculosis should receive isoniazid for 3 months16 after which time the infant should be re-evaluated. BCG vaccination is recommended by WHO and in the UK when isoniazid is stopped.16 • Co-infection with HIV increases the risk of patients de- veloping both pulmonary and extrapulmonary tuberculo- sis, and mortality is higher than in HIV-negative patients in the absence of antiretroviral therapy. HIV patients (includ- ing children) with tuberculosis have a similar response to short-course chemotherapy as HIV-negative tuberculosis patients and most can be treated with the standard 6-month regimen (RHZE2/RH4).4,17-20 In children and patients whose clinical or bacteriological response is slow, treat- ment should be extended to a total of 9 months.18-20 Chil- dren with extrapulmonary tuberculosis involving the bones or CNS, or in those with miliary disease, should be given treatment for a minimum of 12 months.18 Treatment failures in HIV-infected patients have been associated with reduced drug concentrations due to malabsorption of an- timycobacterials.21 Most clinicians would defer starting antiretroviral therapy in HIV co-infected patients with CD4+ counts greater than 200/microlitre
